title: The snowstorm behind the preacher
hook: Emerson recalls a sermon so hollow that the real snow falling outside the window preached better (Divinity School Address)

segments.voice: Yesterday, The American Scholar: Emerson asking people to read books without letting books do all their thinking. Your line was think for myself. What did you work out on your own? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-two.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once sat through a sermon so lifeless, he says, that it nearly tempted him to stop going to church altogether. The minister went on, correct and hollow. Behind him was a window, and through the window, snow was falling. Emerson's eye kept leaving the pulpit for the weather. Later, standing in front of a room of young men about to become ministers themselves, he told them about that sermon. What he remembered was the snow.
screen: `A HOLLOW SERMON.` → `SNOW THROUGH THE WINDOW.` → `THE SNOW IS WHAT HE REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: First, the line itself. The talk is known as the Divinity School Address, given at Harvard. Emerson tells it plainly. A snow storm was falling around them, and then comes the sentence: "The snow storm was real; the preacher merely spectral." Spectral. Like a ghost. There, and not there. Second, what was missing. Emerson says you couldn't tell from the sermon that the man had ever lived. Not one word hinted that he had laughed or cried, married or fallen in love, been praised or cheated or embarrassed. Whatever his life had taught him, none of it made it into the room. The words were about faith, and they were empty of the man. Third, what Emerson wanted instead. He says a true preacher hands out his own life to people, life passed through the fire of thought. And this is worth saying fairly: in the same address he calls the Sabbath and the institution of preaching two great gifts Christianity gave the world. His complaint is not with church. It's with a speaker who talks about holy things from a long way off. Fourth, why the snow. The snow didn't say anything. It just fell, fully there, and so it taught better than the sermon did. That's a test anyone can borrow: when you speak about what matters to you, does it come from what you've lived, or from what you've heard is the right thing to say? The snow was real. It's a high bar, and a plain one.
screen: `THE SNOW STORM WAS REAL.` · `NOT ONE WORD OF HIS OWN LIFE.` · `LIFE PASSED THROUGH THOUGHT.` · `THE SNOW TAUGHT BETTER.` · then, large: `THE PREACHER MERELY SPECTRAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what's real right now. Settle, and let the breath go at its own pace. Then let your attention go to whatever is actually here, the way Emerson's went to the window. The weight of your body in the chair. A sound from outside. The temperature of the air on your hands. The light, whatever it's doing. No commentary, no meaning to find. Just the plain fact of each thing, fully there, like snow falling. When a thought pulls you off, notice it, and come back to one real thing. The bell holds the time.
The snowstorm behind the preacher. Emerson's memory of a hollow sermon, and the real snow falling past the window that said more than the man in the pulpit. Today's word.
screen: `THE SNOWSTORM BEHIND THE PREACHER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the snow was real. Once today, when you catch yourself saying something you've only heard, stop and say what you've actually seen instead. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Readers of Emerson often return to the snowstorm passage as a test for any speaker or teacher: whether what they say has passed through their own life, or only through other people's words.
